title: Drupal site settings over JSON:API, per consumer
description: Four years ago I wrote that Drupal's JSON:API had no way to reach basic site configuration, and guessed the answer would involve Consumers and theme settings. It turns out it did. Decoupled Settings exposes the config Drupal already holds, and lets every frontend override just the bits it needs.

content.html:
Back in April 2022 I wrote about decoupling configuration with Config Pages. It opened with a complaint:

While the Drupal JSON:API still doesn't provide any way to access basic site configuration, there are many ways it can be done...

And it ended with a guess at where I'd go next:

One of my future experiments with Druxt will be to look at the options of using the Drupal Consumers module alongside Drupal theme settings as a solution.

Four years is a long time to leave an experiment sitting there. It's now a module: Decoupled Settings, first beta on Drupal.org this week.

I said in my last post that File (Field) Paths was next up, and it still is. This one just kept nagging at me until I wrote it.

Core's JSON:API is a content API. Nodes, terms, users, media. It has never exposed simple configuration, and honestly it probably shouldn't by default, because a fair bit of what lives in system.site is nobody's business.

But a decoupled frontend still needs the boring stuff. Site name for the document title. Slogan. Logo and favicon. The front page path, so the router knows what "home" means. Every decoupled Drupal project I've built has solved that itself, and mostly solved it by putting a second copy of the site name somewhere.

paragraphs.title: Isn't that what Config Pages is for?

content.html:
Sort of, and I'm not walking away from it. Config Pages is still installed on my sites and I'd still reach for it tomorrow.

What it's for is settings you invent. The 2022 post was about a single page app being fed configuration data from Drupal, and that's exactly the job: define a Config Page type, add whatever fields the app needs, done. Nothing has changed there.

Where it gets awkward is settings Drupal already stores. Model the site name as a field on a Config Page and the site name now exists in two places, and something has to keep them in step, and sooner or later something won't. That's the bit I wanted to stop doing.

paragraphs.title: Read it in place, override it sparsely

content.html: So the module doesn't store settings. It reads them from the config objects that already hold them, and a consumer stores only what it changes.

content.alt: The per-consumer overrides form for a consumer named Partner Portal, showing a Setting column, an Inherited value column, an Override checkbox and a Value for this consumer field. system.site:name and system.site:slogan are ticked and overridden; langcode, page.403, page.404 and page.front are unticked and inherited.
content.caption: Two settings overridden, four inherited. The unticked rows follow the site value whenever an editor changes it.

content.html:
That's the whole model. Tick a setting, give it a value, and this consumer sees your value. Leave it unticked and it keeps following the site, so overriding one frontend's name doesn't freeze its front page path.

The one subtlety worth knowing: an override set to an empty value is a value. If a consumer should show no slogan at all, tick it and leave it blank, and that's what it gets. Clearing the override is a separate action, and that's what restores inheritance. Every settings system I've built before this one collapsed those two into one and I've regretted it every time.

paragraphs.title: What can a frontend actually read?

content.html: Only what you list, and within that, only what typed config schema declares. On install that's system.site plus the active theme, and nothing else.

content.alt: The Decoupled Settings configuration form, showing an Exposed configuration list containing system.site, a checkbox to expose the active theme settings, an Excluded settings box containing system.site:mail, and a 'What a frontend will read' table listing each exposed setting with its global value.
content.caption: The exposure list is the security boundary, and the table underneath shows what a frontend would get right now, unsaved changes included.

content.html: Reading it needs the Read decoupled settings permission, which is not granted to anonymous on install. That's deliberate: the module does nothing until you've decided whether these values are public. If they are, grant it to anonymous. If they're not, grant it to a role behind an OAuth2 scope. system.site:mail is excluded out of the box, because no frontend needs the site email address and plenty of bots want it.

The logo and favicon come back as resolved URLs, through core's own theme settings resolution and its fallbacks, rather than raw config paths the frontend has to interpret. Responses carry the cache tags of every config object that contributed, so changing the site name invalidates them without anyone writing a hook.

paragraphs.title: The OAuth client is the consumer

content.html:
This is the part I enjoyed most, and I can't take credit for it, because it falls out of how Simple OAuth and Consumers already fit together.

Ask for a client_credentials token, then just use it. No consumerId, no header. Simple OAuth puts the token's own consumer on the request, so the app is identified by the token alone. The OAuth client and the settings consumer turn out to be the same entity doing both jobs, which is the sort of thing that makes you suspect you're finally on the right track.

One backend, many frontends, each one rendering as its own site.

There's a companion Druxt module in review that does the frontend half: at build time it identifies itself as a consumer, reads the endpoint, and bakes the result into the build, title and favicon included. Run the same repository twice with two different consumer IDs and you get two differently branded sites out of it. Nothing in the code differs between them.

Which is funny, because the 2022 post said I found the other side of that coin more interesting: one frontend, many backends. Four years on, it's the first one people keep asking me for.

It's 1.0.0-beta1, and the beta is real rather than decorative. Before I'd call it stable I want per-consumer include and exclude lists either built or deliberately deferred, a second real consumer of the API that isn't my own Druxt module, and some soak time on sites that aren't mine.

Two things it doesn't do, and won't quietly start doing: you can't serve public basics and authenticated extras from the same site at once, and translated settings aren't handled at all.

What it does have is 89 tests and 435 assertions passing on both Drupal 10 and Drupal 11, and a first DrupalCI run that came back green across all eight jobs, which I'm choosing to enjoy rather than examine too closely.

Now I'll go and finish File (Field) Paths.

content.description: Issue queue on Drupal.org, mirror on GitHub. If you're running decoupled Drupal and you've already solved site settings some other way, tell me how before the API shape sets in a stable release.
